description: Part I of the Indian Constitution (Articles 1 to 4) deals with the Union and its Territory. It covers the geographical integration of India, the admission or establishment of new states, and the reorganization of existing states.

sections.title: Articles of Part I of the Constitution
sections.description: Constitutional provisions regarding the name of the Union, the establishment of new states, and the alteration of boundaries.

key_concepts.explanation: The 'Territory of India' is a wider expression than the 'Union of India', as the latter includes only states, while the former includes states, Union Territories, and any territory that may be acquired by the Government of India at any future time.

polity_articles.provision: India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
polity_articles.details: The Constituent Assembly preferred the term 'Union' over 'Federation' because the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among the states, and the states have no right to secede from the federation.

polity_articles.provision: Admission or establishment of new States.
polity_articles.details: Empowers Parliament to admit into the Union of India, or establish, new states on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit (applicable to territories not already part of India, e.g., Sikkim initially).

polity_articles.provision: Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries, or names of existing States.
polity_articles.details: A bill for this purpose can be introduced in Parliament only with the prior recommendation of the President, who must refer the bill to the concerned State Legislature for expressing its views.

polity_articles.provision: Laws made under Articles 2 and 3 are not to be considered Constitutional Amendments under Article 368.
polity_articles.details: Such laws can be passed by Parliament by a simple majority and through the ordinary legislative process.

sections.title: Reorganization of States on a Linguistic Basis
sections.description: The post-independence demands to reorganize states on a linguistic basis and the various commissions formed to address this issue.

historical_events.significance: The Linguistic Provinces Commission under S.K. Dhar recommended the reorganization of states on the basis of administrative convenience rather than linguistic factors.
Consisting of Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, and Pattabhi Sitaramayya, this committee formally rejected language as the basis for the reorganization of states.
The first linguistic state was created by separating the Telugu-speaking areas from the Madras State. This followed the death of Potti Sriramulu after a 56-day hunger strike.
A 3-member States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar, and H.N. Kunzru) broadly accepted language as the basis of reorganization but rejected the theory of 'one language-one state'.

sections.title: States Reorganisation Act 1956
sections.description: The comprehensive reorganization of Indian states based on the Fazl Ali Commission's recommendations.

key_concepts.concept: Abolition of the four-fold classification of states
key_concepts.explanation: The original Constitution classified states into Part A, B, C, and D. The 1956 Act abolished this distinction, establishing 14 States and 6 Union Territories.
Statutory bodies established under the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 (not constitutional bodies). The country is divided into 5 Zonal Councils, each chaired by the Union Home Minister.

polity_articles.provision: Implementation of the States Reorganisation Act.
polity_articles.details: Abolished the distinction between Part B and Part C states and extensively amended the First Schedule of the Constitution.

sections.title: Formation of New States - Chronology
sections.description: The chronological order of the creation of important states in the Indian Union post-1956.

historical_events.significance: The bilingual state of Bombay was divided into two separate states: Maharashtra for Marathi-speaking people and Gujarat (the 15th state) for Gujarati-speaking people.
Created as the 16th state by taking the Naga Hills and Tuensang area out of the state of Assam.
On the recommendation of the Shah Commission, the State of Punjab was bifurcated to create Haryana (the 17th state) and the Union Territory of Chandigarh.
The rule of the Chogyal dynasty ended, and Sikkim was integrated as the 22nd full-fledged state of the Indian Union.

historical_events.event: Formation of Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, and Jharkhand
historical_events.significance: Created out of the territories of Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, and Bihar respectively, becoming the 26th, 27th, and 28th states of India.
Carved out of the territory of Andhra Pradesh as the 29th state of the Indian Union.

sections.title: Important Facts and Recent Changes
sections.description: Key constitutional facts and recent administrative changes related to the Union and its territories.

polity_articles.details: The 35th Amendment (1974) conferred 'Associate State' status to Sikkim (inserted Article 2A). The 36th Amendment (1975) made it a full state and repealed Article 2A.
Redesignated the Union Territory of Delhi as the 'National Capital Territory of Delhi' (NCT) and provided for a legislative assembly and a council of ministers.

important_facts.fact: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 bifurcated the state of Jammu and Kashmir into two separate Union Territories: Jammu & Kashmir, and Ladakh, bringing the number of states down to 28.
In 2020, the Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu were merged into a single Union Territory, bringing the current total to 28 States and 8 Union Territories in India.
